_readme: Curated field/lab footage, with the licence obligations attached to the media.
Every entry here was verified against the Wikimedia Commons API: the file
exists, the direct URL resolves, and the licence and author are as recorded.
CC BY and CC BY-SA REQUIRE attribution, so `attribution` and `source_url` are
not decoration -- the app renders them next to the player, and the ingest
script refuses to register a clip that is missing either.
On 360 footage: genuine 360-degree capture of crop disease is not available
under a reusable licence. It essentially does not exist yet -- the closest
published work is the TNAU downy-mildew VR module, which is not distributed.
So the real clips below are flat, and in the headset they play on a WebXR
quad layer, which is the correct way to show flat video in VR. One synthetic
equirect clip is kept so the 360 code path stays exercised until real
Transcoding to HLS creates a derivative. For CC BY-SA that means the
derivative carries the same licence -- fine here, worth knowing before this

Still uncovered: Tomato bacterial spot and tomato mosaic virus. No reusable footage of either exists on Commons -- a bacterium and a mechanically transmitted virus are both hard to film. The fungal-infection clip is NOT mapped to them, because it would be showing the wrong kind of pathogen.

videos.title: Phytophthora zoospores swimming
videos.caption: Motile zoospores released from a sporangium. This is stage 4 of the cycle: below about 15 °C the sporangium releases these instead of germinating directly, and they need free water on the leaf to swim. Take the water away and the epidemic stops here.
videos.attribution: Shaikhul Islam Shaokin, via Wikimedia Commons
videos.note: P. capsici, a close relative of P. infestans; the zoospore behaviour is the same.

videos.title: Two-spotted spider mites on a leaf
videos.caption: Adults and eggs on the leaf underside. Each puncture empties one cell, which is what produces the fine pale stippling. Note that these thrive in hot dry air — the opposite of every fungus in this dataset.

videos.title: The virus changes how its whitefly feeds
videos.caption: Bemisia tabaci feeding on an infected plant. TYLCV alters the insect's feeding behaviour in ways that increase transmission — the pathogen manipulating its own vector, which is why controlling the whitefly is the only control for the disease.
videos.attribution: Moreno-Delafuente A, Garzo E, Moreno A, Fereres A (2013), PLoS ONE, via Wikimedia Commons

videos.title: Whiteflies on the leaf underside
videos.caption: The vector at rest and disturbed. A whitefly that has fed on an infected plant for 15-30 minutes stays infectious for the rest of its life, which is why a crop-free period between plantings matters more than spraying.

videos.title: A fungus delivering effectors into a host cell
videos.caption: Live imaging of effector trafficking inside a fungal hypha during infection. This is stage 6 — the fungus is inside the tissue suppressing the plant's defences, and nothing is visible on the leaf yet. That invisible window is why a protectant spray has to go on before the wetting event, not after symptoms appear.
videos.attribution: Bielska E, Higuchi Y, Schuster M, Steinberg N, Kilaru S, Talbot NJ, Steinberg G (2014), Nature Communications, via Wikimedia Commons

videos.title: Powdery mildew colonising a leaf surface
videos.caption: Mildew growth on a susceptible host compared with a resistant one. Unlike most fungi here, powdery mildew does not need free water to germinate — high humidity is enough, which is why it appears in dry weather when other diseases do not.
videos.attribution: Zheng Z, Nonomura T, Appiano M, Pavan S, Matsuda Y, Toyoda H, et al. (2013), PLoS ONE, via Wikimedia Commons

videos.title: Biological control of powdery mildew
videos.caption: A biocontrol agent applied against Podosphaera xanthii. An intervention acting on the colonisation stage rather than on the spore, which is why timing it is different from timing a protectant fungicide.
videos.attribution: Gafni A, Calderon C, Harris R, Buxdorf K, Dafa-Berger A, Zeilinger-Reichert E, Levy M (2015), via Wikimedia Commons

videos.title: Orchard walk-through (placeholder)
videos.caption: A synthetic equirectangular pattern standing in for real orchard capture. It exists so the 360 code path — equirect layer, sphere fallback, look-around — stays exercised. Replace it with real footage shot on a 360 camera; the pipeline does not change.
videos.attribution: Generated by tools/transcode.sh from an ffmpeg test pattern

videos.title: Flying through a fruit orchard
videos.caption: A drone flight between the rows of a cherry orchard, at canopy height. This is the setting, not the disease: it is what an orchard's spacing and canopy density actually look like, which is the thing pruning and row spacing change. An open canopy dries after rain; a closed one holds the leaf wetness that scab and black rot need.
videos.download: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Cherry trees in an orchard as viewed from FPV drone.webm
videos.note: Cherry orchard, not apple. Labelled as setting rather than as the crop, because it is not the crop.

videos.title: Seedlings emerging — time-lapse
videos.caption: A time-lapse of two seedlings germinating and opening their first leaves. This is the host leg of the disease triangle: no susceptible host, no disease. It is also the window that matters most for late blight, because a seedling infected early produces almost nothing.
